title: Serverless & Containers
oneLiner: Run code without servers and ship containers without clusters: Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, ECS, EKS, and Fargate.
examWeightNote: Serverless and container patterns span High-Performing, Resilient, and Cost-Optimized designs.
objectives: Build serverless APIs with Lambda behind API Gateway, and know Lambda's limits.
Orchestrate multi-step workflows with Step Functions (Standard vs Express).
Contrast ECS and EKS, and the EC2 vs Fargate launch types.
Know when serverless beats containers beats EC2 for a given workload.

services.name: AWS Lambda
services.purpose: Run event-driven functions with no servers; pay per request and duration (up to a 15-minute timeout).

services.name: Amazon API Gateway
services.purpose: Managed REST/HTTP/WebSocket API front door — auth, throttling, and routing to Lambda or other backends.

services.name: AWS Step Functions
services.purpose: Serverless workflow orchestration (state machine) with retries, branching, and parallelism.

services.name: Amazon ECS
services.purpose: AWS-native container orchestration; runs tasks on EC2 or on serverless Fargate.

services.name: Amazon EKS
services.purpose: Managed Kubernetes for teams that want the Kubernetes ecosystem/portability.

services.name: AWS Fargate
services.purpose: Serverless compute for ECS/EKS — run containers without managing EC2 hosts.

keyConcepts: Lambda suits short (≤15 min), event-driven, spiky work with zero idle cost; it scales automatically. Long-running or specialized workloads belong on containers or EC2.
A classic serverless API: API Gateway (routing, auth, throttling) → Lambda (logic) → DynamoDB/RDS. Add Cognito for user auth.
Step Functions coordinates multiple Lambdas/services into a reliable workflow with built-in retries and error handling — Standard for long-running/durable, Express for high-volume short flows.
ECS is AWS-native and simpler; EKS gives you managed Kubernetes and portability. Both can run on EC2 (you manage hosts) or Fargate (serverless).
Fargate removes server management and right-sizes per task, but EC2 launch type can be cheaper at steady high scale (and allows GPUs/special instances).
Store images in Amazon ECR; for very simple containerized web apps, AWS App Runner offers an even more hands-off option.

diagram.caption: A serverless API on the left; containers (EC2 vs Fargate) on the right.
diagram.note: Pick by workload: spiky/short/event-driven → Lambda; long-running or portable → containers; steady heavy scale → maybe EC2 launch type.

scenarios.scenario: A team needs a REST API for a mobile app with unpredictable, spiky traffic. They want zero idle cost and no servers to manage.
scenarios.question: Which architecture fits best?

options.label: Amazon API Gateway in front of AWS Lambda (with DynamoDB)
A fleet of always-on EC2 instances
A single large EC2 with a public IP

scenarios.explanation: API Gateway + Lambda is the serverless API pattern: it scales automatically with spiky traffic, costs nothing when idle, and needs no servers. Always-on EC2/EKS incur idle cost and management overhead.

scenarios.scenario: A company has containerized microservices and wants to run them without provisioning, patching, or scaling EC2 hosts.
scenarios.question: Which option meets this?

options.label: Run ECS or EKS on AWS Fargate
Run ECS on the EC2 launch type and manage the instances
Deploy each container to its own Lambda layer

scenarios.explanation: Fargate is the serverless launch type for ECS/EKS — you run containers without managing the underlying hosts. The EC2 launch type would require you to manage the instances.

quiz.question: Which workload is the best fit for AWS Lambda?
options: A process that must run continuously for hours
Short, event-driven, spiky tasks that should cost nothing when idle
A workload needing a specific GPU for days
A monolith that can't be changed
quiz.answer: Short, event-driven, spiky tasks that should cost nothing when idle
quiz.explanation: Lambda is ideal for short (≤15 min), event-driven, bursty work with no idle cost and automatic scaling.

quiz.question: What does Amazon API Gateway provide in a serverless API?
options: A managed API front door with routing, auth, and throttling (often to Lambda)
A relational database
Container orchestration
A CDN cache only
quiz.answer: A managed API front door with routing, auth, and throttling (often to Lambda)
quiz.explanation: API Gateway handles REST/HTTP/WebSocket APIs — routing, authorization, and throttling — commonly in front of Lambda.

quiz.question: AWS Step Functions is used to:
options: Store container images
Orchestrate multi-step workflows with retries and branching across services
Serve static web content
Encrypt data at rest
quiz.answer: Orchestrate multi-step workflows with retries and branching across services
quiz.explanation: Step Functions coordinates Lambdas/services into durable state-machine workflows with built-in error handling (Standard vs Express).

quiz.question: What is the difference between the ECS EC2 and Fargate launch types?
options: EC2 launch type means you manage the host instances; Fargate is serverless (no hosts to manage)
Fargate requires you to patch servers; EC2 does not
They are identical
Fargate only runs on-premises
quiz.answer: EC2 launch type means you manage the host instances; Fargate is serverless (no hosts to manage)
quiz.explanation: With the EC2 launch type you provision/patch/scale the cluster instances; Fargate removes that by running tasks serverlessly.

quiz.question: When would you choose Amazon EKS over Amazon ECS?
options: When you want the Kubernetes ecosystem and portability
When you never want to use containers
When you need a relational database
When you want to avoid all orchestration
quiz.answer: When you want the Kubernetes ecosystem and portability
quiz.explanation: EKS is managed Kubernetes — pick it for Kubernetes tooling/portability; ECS is simpler and AWS-native.

quiz.question: Where are container images stored for ECS/EKS on AWS?
options: Amazon ECR (Elastic Container Registry)
Amazon S3 Glacier
AWS Secrets Manager
Amazon Athena
quiz.explanation: ECR is AWS's managed container image registry, integrated with ECS, EKS, and IAM.

quiz.question: A key limit of AWS Lambda to remember is:
options: It can run for a maximum of 15 minutes per invocation
It can only run once per day
It cannot be triggered by events
It requires you to manage servers
quiz.answer: It can run for a maximum of 15 minutes per invocation
quiz.explanation: Lambda functions have a 15-minute maximum execution time; longer jobs should use containers, Batch, or EC2.
